candidates.bio: Rabbi Yochanan b. Gudgada was a Levite sage of the first generation of Tannaim. He served in the Second Temple and was among the Levites appointed to lock its gates.

Rabbi Yochanan b. Torta was a third-generation Tanna of the early 2nd century CE and a close friend of Rabbi Akiva. He is remembered for opposing Bar Kokhba, notably challenging Rabbi Akiva's messianic application of "A star shall go forth from Jacob" (Numbers 24:17) to him. Only two statements of his are preserved in rabbinic literature. Aggadic tradition associates him with the legend of a Shabbat-observant cow that inspired a gentile's conversion; some versions identify him as the convert who took the name ben Torta ("son of the cow").

Rabbi Yochanan deKatzion, also called deKartzion, was an Eretz Yisraeli Amora whose exact period is unknown, though he likely belonged to the second generation of Amoraim. Shlomo Sirilio, an early commentator on the Jerusalem Talmud, proposed that his name should be read as Rabbi Yochanan deKisaryon, indicating an origin in Caesarea.

R. Yohanan Hasandlar was born in Egypt, but moved to the Land of Israel where he became a devoted student of R. Akiva. Even when the latter was in a Roman jail, R. Yochanan found a way to come to him for instruction.

R. Yochanan studied under R. Yehudah haNasi and emerged as the next leader after his death. He directed the academy in Tiberias and set up the groundwork for the Jerusalem Talmud. His unusual beauty, sharpness and personal sufferings made him a captivating yet intimidating teacher. It was due to his personality and his unrivaled learning that the center of Torah study did not move to Babylonia during his lifetime.

candidates.bio: R. Yishmael b. Yohanan b. Berokah was a contemporary of R. Shimon b. Gamliel and is often cited together with him.
R. Yohanan b. Nuri was a brilliant and pious member of Rabban Gamliel's academy in Yavneh. After finding out about his desperate poverty, R. Gamliel promoted him.

Rabbi Yochanan b. ha-Chorani was a Tanna who lived in the generation between the era of the Pairs and the era of the Tannaim. He was a student of Shammai the Elder, yet in practice he followed the rulings of Beit Hillel all his life. He was the teacher of Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Zadok. The accepted view is that his name indicates that he or one of his parents dwelt in the city of Choran in Syria, though some claim he lived in Beit Choron.

candidates.bio: Yose b. Yoezer and Yose b. Yochanan served as the first of the zugot (pairs), with the first being Nasi (religious leader) and the second the head of the court. They served after Antigonos in a period of intense Hellenization and war, and promulgated several leniencies to encourage Jews to keep the law under these difficult conditions.

Yochanan (John Hyrkanus) the High Priest was the son of Shimon the Hasmonean and succeeded him as high priest and political leader. He fought several wars against the Syrian Greeks and local enemies. Among them were the Idumeans whom he forced to convert. Though loyal to the Pharisees most of his life, he was finally seduced into joining with the Sadducees.

Rabbi Yochanan b. Beroka was a third-generation Tanna and student of Rabbi Yehoshua b. Hananiah, and a colleague of Rabbi Elazar b. Hisma. Several laws in the Mishnah and many baraitot are cited in his name, often together with Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon. His statement in Avot concerns desecration of God's name. He innovated a ruling that one may redirect an inheritance among heirs of the same gender category fit to inherit, and the halakha follows his opinion. He also ruled that a man must allot provisions for his daughters after his death. Distinctively, he held that the commandment of procreation applies to women as well as men, based on the word "them" in the biblical verse. His son, Rabbi Yishmael, was also a sage whose teachings appear in Avot and in baraitot.

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was a first-century Jewish leader and scholar who oversaw the fragile transition of the Jewish people to life without a [Temple](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/beit-hamikdash?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources), upon the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE at the hands of the Romans. While he sought accommodation with the Romans, he was unable to convince the faction of zealots to give up their position, which ultimately led to the destruction of [Jerusalem](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/jerusalem?tab=admin). Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's students smuggled him out of Jerusalem, enabling him to renew Jewish life and learning from [Yavneh](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yavneh?tab=admin). Yochanan ben Dahavai was a tanna of the land of Israel who does not appear in the Mishnah but is cited in several baraitot across the Bavli, Tosefta, and Sifra. He transmits halakhot in the name of Rabbi Yehuda (bar Ilai) — most prominently the ruling that a person blind in one eye is exempt from the pilgrimage obligation of 're'iyah' (appearance at the Temple), derived from reading the verse 'yera'eh/yir'eh' (Exodus 23:17) as requiring two-way seeing (Chagigah 2a, 4b; Arakhin 2b; Tosefta Chagigah 1:2; Sanhedrin 4b, where the source is given as Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima). The Tosefta records that Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) responded against his view and that the Sages decided in favor of Rabbi Yehuda's position. He also gives an opinion on the dyeing of tekhelet (Menachot 42b) and a related exegesis of 'shni tola'at' (Sifra, Metzora 1), and is the author of the rejected teaching in Nedarim 20a on marital conduct. The name 'Dahavai' (from Aramaic 'dahava', gold) is widely regarded as an epithet rather than a birth name, perhaps reflecting a goldsmith father or a wordplay on one of his teachings (R. Reuven Margaliot, Shemot ve-Kinuyim ba-Talmud).
